events.title: Early Human Settlement
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows humans began settling present-day Colombia at the end of the last Ice Age. Stone tools and animal remains found at El Abra rock shelter in Boyacá prove existence of early hunter-gatherers. These early inhabitants tracked large mammals like mastodons and ancient horses.

events.title: Agricultural Revolution
events.description: Colombian region began agricultural practices, cultivating maize, cassava, beans and squash. Pottery-making techniques emerged, archaeologists discovered some of Americas' oldest pottery at Puerto Hormiga and San Jacinto, dating to 3000 BCE. Agricultural development led to more stable settlements and population growth.

events.title: Quimbaya Culture Emerges
events.description: Quimbaya culture flourished in Cauca River valley region. They were renowned for exquisite goldwork, creating intricate gold artifacts, anthropomorphic figures and ritual objects. Quimbaya artisans mastered lost-wax casting and gold-copper alloy techniques. Their work displayed high artistic and technical achievement, masterpieces seen today at Bogotá's Gold Museum.

events.title: San Agustín Culture
events.description: San Agustín region developed unique megalithic culture, carving large stone statues, tombs and religious monuments. These mysterious stone sculptures depicted deities, animals and human figures, possessing complex cosmology and religious beliefs. San Agustín Archaeological Park is Colombia's most important archaeological site, listed as World Heritage. Culture continued until around 900 CE.

events.title: Tairona Civilization
events.description: Tairona people established advanced civilization in Santa Marta mountains of Colombia's northern Caribbean coast. They built complex stone cities, terraced farms and irrigation systems. Ciudad Perdida (Lost City/Teyuna) built around 800 CE was Tairona's most important urban center, featuring stone staircases, plazas and residential platforms. Tairona were skilled goldsmiths, potters and weavers.

events.title: Muisca Confederation Formation
events.description: Muisca people established complex political organization in Andean highlands of Cundinamarca and Boyacá regions. They formed two main confederations: northern Zaque ruling Tunja area, southern Zipa ruling Bacatá area. Muisca society was highly stratified with nobility, priests and commoner classes. They developed unique calendar system and religious rituals.

events.title: Muisca Economic Prosperity
events.description: Muisca developed complex economic system, despite not using currency, they established extensive trade networks. They exchanged salt, emeralds and textiles with neighboring tribes for gold, cacao and tropical fruits. Muisca mined salt at Zipaquirá and Nemocón, salt became important trading commodity. They were also skilled farmers, using terraces and irrigation to grow maize, potatoes and marigolds.

events.title: Lake Guatavita Ritual Tradition
events.description: Muisca developed famous religious ritual at Lake Guatavita, where new Zipa would be covered in gold dust, ride raft to lake center, throw gold and emeralds into lake as offerings. This ritual later became origin of El Dorado legend, attracting countless Spanish conquistadors seeking legendary golden city. Muisca believed Lake Guatavita was sacred place, linked to their creation myths.

events.title: First European Contact
events.description: Spanish explorers Alonso de Ojeda and Juan de la Cosa first explored Colombian Caribbean coast. Italian navigator Amerigo Vespucci also participated in this expedition. They discovered indigenous stilt houses, naming area 'Little Venice' (Venezuela). This marked beginning of European contact with Colombian region.

events.title: San Sebastián Founded
events.description: Spanish conquistador Alonso de Ojeda established San Sebastián de Urabá at Gulf of Urabá, first European settlement on present Colombian territory. However, colony quickly failed due to indigenous resistance, disease and food shortages. Survivors fled to Santa María la Antigua del Darién.

events.title: Santa Marta Founded
events.description: Spanish conquistador Rodrigo de Bastidas established Santa Marta on Caribbean coast, Colombia's oldest surviving city. Santa Marta became important base for Spanish conquest of interior. City had conflictual relationship with Tairona indigenous people, Spanish attempted to control region's gold resources.

events.title: Cartagena Founded
events.description: Pedro de Heredia established Cartagena de Indias, city quickly became one of Spanish America's most important ports. Cartagena with its excellent harbor became gathering point for Spanish fleets and crucial hub for shipping gold and silver from Americas to Europe. To defend against pirate attacks, Spanish built magnificent fortifications including San Felipe Castle.

events.title: Jiménez de Quesada Expedition
events.description: Spanish conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada led expedition from Santa Marta, ascending Magdalena River into Andean highlands seeking El Dorado. Expedition endured hardships, crossing jungles, mountains and swamps, finally reaching Sabana plateau inhabited by Muisca people. This expedition opened conquest of Muisca civilization.

events.title: Conquest of Muisca Civilization
events.description: Jiménez de Quesada conquered Muisca confederation, capturing Zipa Bogotá and plundering Bacatá's gold and emeralds. Despite Muisca numerical superiority, internal divisions and lack of horses and firearms prevented effective resistance against Spanish. Conquest led to Muisca political system collapse, population greatly reduced by war and disease. Muisca gold wealth became important source for Spanish colonial finances.

events.title: Santafé de Bogotá Founded
events.description: Jiménez de Quesada established Santafé de Bogotá on Muisca Zipa's former territory, commemorating Spain's Santa Fe and Muisca ruler Bogotá's name. City built on Cundinamarca plateau at 2,640 meters elevation, enjoying mild climate and fertile land. Bogotá became New Granada colony's administrative center, later developing into Colombia Republic's capital.

events.title: Royal Audiencia of New Granada
events.description: Spanish Crown established Royal Audiencia de Santa Fe de Bogotá as Bogotá's supreme judicial and administrative body. Audiencia responsible for judicial affairs, protecting indigenous rights (at least theoretically) and overseeing colonial officials. This marked Spanish establishment of formal colonial administrative system in region. New Granada initially under Viceroyalty of Peru jurisdiction.

events.title: Popayán Province Established
events.description: Spanish established Provincia de Popayán, governing vast region of southern and western Colombia, including present-day Cauca, Nariño, parts of Cauca Valley and northern Ecuador. Popayán city became important colonial administrative center, known for white architecture and conservative aristocratic society. Region rich in gold deposits, attracting numerous Spanish settlers and African slave labor.

events.title: Drake Attacks Cartagena
events.description: English pirate Francis Drake led massive fleet attacking Cartagena, besieging for weeks and demanding huge ransom. Though Drake eventually left, attack exposed Cartagena's defensive weaknesses. Spanish subsequently invested heavily in strengthening defenses, building stronger walls, fortresses and Castillo de San Felipe de Barajas, making Cartagena one of Spanish America's most fortified cities.

events.title: African Slave Rebellion
events.description: Near Cartagena, African slaves under Benkos Biohó's leadership launched large-scale rebellion, escaping plantations and mines. They established free towns (palenques) in swamps and jungles, most famous being San Basilio de Palenque. These maroon communities successfully resisted multiple Spanish expeditions, maintaining independence and preserving African cultural traditions to present day.

events.title: Viceroyalty of New Granada Established
events.description: Spanish Crown established Virreinato de Nueva Granada with capital Bogotá, independent from Viceroyalty of Peru. Viceroyalty included present-day Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama. This elevated Bogotá's political status, making it most important administrative center of northern South America. Viceroyalty establishment aimed at more effective regional governance and increased tax revenue.

events.title: Vernon Attacks Cartagena
events.description: British Admiral Edward Vernon led massive fleet (186 ships and about 23,600 men) besieging Cartagena, one of 18th century's largest amphibious operations. However, Spanish garrison under General Blas de Lezo's heroic leadership, relying on Cartagena's strong fortifications, successfully repelled British. British retreated with heavy casualties from disease and wounds. This victory considered one of Spanish America's greatest military victories.

events.title: Comunero Revolt
events.description: Socorro region erupted in Revolución de los Comuneros, protesting Spanish tax increases and monopoly policies. Thousands of Creoles, mestizos and indigenous people under José Antonio Galán and others marched toward Bogotá. Though viceroy initially promised reforms, revolt ultimately suppressed, leaders executed. Comunero Revolt presaged social discontent of later independence movement.

events.title: Antonio Nariño and Rights of Man
events.description: Creole intellectual Antonio Nariño secretly translated and printed French Declaration of Rights of Man and Citizen in Bogotá, marking Enlightenment ideas' spread in New Granada. Spanish authorities arrested Nariño, sentencing him to African exile. However, Rights of Man ideas inspired entire generation of Creole elite, laying ideological foundation for independence movement. Nariño later escaped and returned, becoming important independence movement leader.

events.title: Napoleonic Invasion Impact
events.description: Napoleon's invasion of Spain and deposition of King Ferdinand VII created political crisis in Spanish America. New Granada's Creole elite faced loyalty question: support Spanish provisional government, deposed king, or French puppet regime? This crisis provided opportunity for independence movement, regions began forming autonomous juntas, claiming to govern for imprisoned king but actually moving toward autonomy and independence.

events.title: Bogotá Independence Declaration
events.description: In 'Grito' (Vase Incident), Bogotá Creole elite orchestrated conflict with Spanish merchant, triggering popular demonstrations. That day, citizens and Creole leaders assembled in Bogotá's main plaza, establishing Supreme Junta, declaring autonomy and deposing Spanish viceroy. July 20 became Colombia's Independence Day, though actual independence war just beginning. New Granada provinces followed suit, declaring autonomy or independence.

events.title: Cartagena's Complete Independence
events.description: Cartagena under radical Creole push became first New Granada province declaring complete independence from Spain. Cartagena established republican government, promulgated constitution, abolished slavery (one of Americas' earliest abolitions). However, Cartagena's radical stance opposed conservative Bogotá government, causing New Granada internal division, period called 'Patria Boba' (Foolish Fatherland).

events.title: Patria Boba Civil War
events.description: After independence New Granada descended into fierce civil war, federalists (led by Cartagena) versus centralists (led by Bogotá) fighting for control. Provinces established own governments, conflicting with each other. Simón Bolívar attempted mediation but failed. This civil war seriously weakened independence movement, unable to effectively resist Spanish restoration forces. War wasted resources, missing opportunity to consolidate independence.

events.title: Morillo's Bloody Reconquest
events.description: Spanish General Pablo Morillo arrived with 10,000-strong expeditionary force, reconquering New Granada. Morillo besieged Cartagena for 106 days, causing thousands to starve. After capture, Morillo imposed 'Régimen del Terror' (Reign of Terror) in Bogotá and other cities, executing hundreds of independence leaders, intellectuals and suspects. Period called Spanish Restoration, but brutal repression instead sparked stronger independence will.

events.title: Battle of Boyacá
events.description: Simón Bolívar led patriot army from Venezuela crossing Andes during rainy season in bold march, surprising New Granada. Near Puente de Boyacá, patriot army defeated Spanish forces, cutting off retreat. Three days later, Bolívar liberated Bogotá. Battle of Boyacá was decisive victory, securing New Granada independence, paving way for Gran Colombia. Battle demonstrated Bolívar's military genius and troops' resilience.

events.title: Gran Colombia Established
events.description: At Angostura Congress (present Ciudad Bolívar, Venezuela), Simón Bolívar proclaimed establishment of Gran Colombia Republic, unifying New Granada, Venezuela and future Ecuador (then still under Spanish control). Bolívar became president, Francisco de Paula Santander vice president. Gran Colombia embodied Bolívar's dream of Latin American unity, but faced geographic, economic and political challenges.

events.title: Cúcuta Constitution
events.description: Gran Colombia held constituent assembly in Cúcuta, promulgating first constitution. Constitution established centralist republic, Bolívar as president, Santander as vice president. Constitution declared gradual slavery abolition (freeing slave descendants, but existing slaves wait), guaranteed civil liberties, established separation of powers. However, Bolívar considered constitution too idealistic, unsuited for Latin American reality, foreshadowing later conflicts.

events.title: Liberation of Quito and Guayaquil
events.description: General Antonio José de Sucre defeated Spanish forces at Battle of Pichincha, liberating Quito (Ecuador). Ecuador subsequently incorporated into Gran Colombia. Same year, Bolívar met Argentine independence hero José de San Martín in Guayaquil, discussing South America's future, but ideologies clashed. San Martín subsequently withdrew from politics, Bolívar became undisputed leader of South American independence movement.

events.title: Battle of Ayacucho and Peru Liberation
events.description: General Sucre achieved decisive victory at Battle of Ayacucho in Peru, completely defeating Spanish Royal Army. This victory marked end of Spanish military power on South American continent, ensuring South American independence. Bolívar and Gran Colombia played crucial role in liberating Peru and Bolivia. Bolívar reached power and prestige peak, honored as 'Liberator.'

events.title: Congress of Panama
events.description: Bolívar convened American nations congress in Panama, attempting to establish Latin American alliance for common defense and cooperation. This was effort to realize Bolívar's pan-American idealism. However, congress achieved little due to national interest divergences, vast distances and communication difficulties. Only few countries sent delegates, agreements reached went unimplemented. Panama Congress failure presaged Gran Colombia and Bolívar's unification dream difficulties.

events.title: Bogotá Assassination Attempt
events.description: Liberal conspirators opposing Bolívar's authoritarian rule attempted assassination in Bogotá. Lover Manuela Sáenz warned Bolívar who escaped, she was hailed as 'Liberator of the Liberator.' After failed assassination, Bolívar suppressed opposition, including executing Admiral José Prudencio Padilla. This incident deepened political divisions, damaged Bolívar's reputation, revealing Gran Colombia's serious discord.

events.title: Gran Colombia Dissolution
events.description: Facing irreconcilable regional differences, economic difficulties and political opposition, Gran Colombia finally dissolved. Venezuela and Ecuador successively declared independent separation. Bolívar resigned presidency, planning European exile, but health deteriorated en route to Cartagena. New Granada (present Colombia and Panama) continued as independent nation. Bolívar's unification dream shattered, he said in disappointment: 'We have plowed the sea.'

events.title: Death of Simón Bolívar
events.description: Simón Bolívar died from tuberculosis at San Pedro Alejandrino estate near Santa Marta, aged only 47. He died in poverty, illness and political disappointment, his dreamed Gran Colombia already dissolved. However, Bolívar's legacy as South American liberator endures, honored as one of Latin America's greatest heroes. Bolívar's remains later moved to Caracas National Pantheon.

events.title: Republic of New Granada
events.description: After Gran Colombia dissolution, central territory reorganized as República de la Nueva Granada, including present-day Colombia and Panama. Francisco de Paula Santander returned from exile, elected president. Santander promoted liberal reforms including education expansion, religious tolerance and economic modernization. However, nation faced economic difficulties, debt burden and ideological conflicts between conservatives and liberals.

events.title: Liberal and Conservative Parties Form
events.description: New Granada politics divided into two distinct parties: Liberal Party (Partido Liberal) and Conservative Party (Partido Conservador). Liberals supported federalism, church-state separation, free trade and social reform. Conservatives supported centralism, Catholic Church privileges, protectionism and traditional order. This two-party opposition dominated Colombian politics for over century, causing countless civil wars and violent conflicts, profoundly affecting national development.

events.title: Complete Abolition of Slavery
events.description: Under Liberal President José Hilario López leadership, New Granada completely abolished slavery, freeing about 25,000 slaves. This was part of liberal reform agenda, also including expanded suffrage and religious freedom. Abolition welcomed by Afro-Colombians and liberals, but opposed by conservatives and slaveholders. Abolition had profound impact on Pacific coast and Cauca Valley socioeconomic structure.

events.title: Granadine Confederation
events.description: Nation reorganized as Confederación Granadina, then Estados Unidos de Nueva Granada, finally becoming Estados Unidos de Colombia in 1863. This reflected liberal-pushed radical federalism and local autonomy. Provinces became states with extensive self-governance including military organization power. However, extreme decentralization led to weak nation, frequent civil wars between states and parties.

events.title: Rionegro Constitution
events.description: Liberal Party formulated radical new constitution in Rionegro, establishing extremely federalist Estados Unidos de Colombia. Constitution drastically limited central government power, granting nine sovereign states great autonomy including military and fiscal powers. Constitution guaranteed broad civil liberties, implemented church-state separation, weakened Catholic Church influence. Presidential term only two years without reelection. This constitution was one of 19th century Latin America's most liberal, but also caused national chaos and civil wars.

events.title: School War
events.description: Conservatives and Catholic Church opposed Liberal secular education reforms, civil war erupted. Liberal government attempted to establish public education system, reducing Church control over education, provoking fierce Conservative and Church opposition. Conflict caused thousands of deaths, further deepening ideological divisions.

events.title: Coffee Economy Rise
events.description: Coffee became Colombia's main export product, replacing tobacco, cinchona bark and gold. Andean mountains' mild climate and fertile soil were ideal for coffee cultivation. Colombian coffee industry mainly dominated by small farmers and medium-sized farms, unlike other Latin American countries' large plantation systems. Coffee exports brought wealth to nation, promoting railway and infrastructure construction, but also made economy dependent on single export commodity, vulnerable to international price fluctuations.

events.title: Civil War and Rafael Núñez Rise
events.description: Civil war erupted between radical Liberals and moderates (Independents). Conservative leader Rafael Núñez allied with moderate Liberals, defeating radicals. Núñez believed extreme federalism caused national chaos, advocating strong central government. This civil war paved way for fundamental political system transformation, ending Liberal-dominated federal era.

events.title: 1886 Constitution and Regeneration
events.description: Núñez pushed new constitution formulation, abolishing federalism, establishing centralist República de Colombia. Constitution greatly strengthened president and central government power, reduced states to provinces with centrally appointed governors. Catholic Church restored privileged status, became state religion. Presidential term extended to six years. This authoritarian constitution governed Colombia for over century until 1991. Núñez's 'Regeneración' reform ended liberalism experiment, establishing Conservative-dominated system.

events.title: Thousand Days War
events.description: Colombia's most destructive civil war erupted, Liberal uprising against Conservative government. War caused at least 100,000 deaths (2-3% of population), economic collapse, currency devaluation, coffee production disruption. Panama region became fierce battlefield. War ended with Conservative victory, but nation severely damaged. Thousand Days War's chaos and weakening created conditions for Panama separation, becoming catastrophic event in Colombian history.

events.title: Panama Independence
events.description: With US support, Panama separated from Colombia. Colombian Senate rejected treaty allowing US to build canal in Panama, US then supported Panamanian separatists. US warships prevented Colombian troops from suppressing uprising. Panama quickly gained independence, signed canal treaty with US. Panama loss was devastating blow to Colombia, losing strategically and economically important territory. Colombian people harbored resentment toward US, trauma affecting bilateral relations for decades.

events.title: Rafael Reyes Dictatorship
events.description: General Rafael Reyes served as president, implementing authoritarian rule, attempting to stabilize post-Thousand Days War nation. Reyes promoted economic modernization, infrastructure development, encouraged foreign investment, promoted oil and banana industries. He attempted reconciliation with Liberals, appointing Liberals to government. However, Reyes' term extension and authoritarian methods provoked opposition, eventually forced to resign. Despite controversy, Reyes laid foundation for early 20th century economic development.

events.title: Oil Extraction Begins
events.description: Colombia began large-scale commercial oil extraction, mainly in Barrancabermeja region of Magdalena River valley. Foreign companies especially US companies obtained extraction concessions. Oil became important export commodity after coffee, bringing new revenue source to nation. Oil industry development promoted coastal and inland region economic growth, but also sparked controversy about resource sovereignty and foreign control.

events.title: Banana Massacre
events.description: In Santa Marta banana plantation zone, United Fruit Company workers struck demanding better working conditions. Colombian Army opened fire on peaceful demonstrators in Ciénaga, causing massacre. Official claimed single-digit death toll, but witnesses said hundreds or thousands killed. This event became famous scene in Gabriel García Márquez's novel 'One Hundred Years of Solitude.' Banana Massacre revealed foreign company influence on Colombian politics and working class vulnerability.

events.title: Liberal Party Returns to Power
events.description: After nearly 50 years of Conservative domination, Liberal candidate Enrique Olaya Herrera elected president. Conservatives failed due to internal divisions. Liberal return to power opened 'Liberal Republic' period (1930-1946), promoting social and economic reforms including labor rights, land reform and education expansion. Political alternation showed certain maturity of Colombian democracy, but also laid seeds for new political tensions.

events.title: Leticia Conflict with Peru
events.description: Peruvian civilians occupied Colombian Amazon port of Leticia, triggering military conflict between two countries. Colombia under President Olaya mobilized military, dispatching troops through Magdalena and Amazon rivers. Conflict resolved through international mediation, Leticia returned to Colombia. This brief war enhanced national unity and Olaya government prestige, temporarily easing domestic political tensions.

events.title: Alfonso López Reforms
events.description: Liberal President Alfonso López Pumarejo promoted 'Revolución en Marcha' reform program. Reforms included land reform, expanded labor rights, universal education, weakened Church monopoly on education and expanded suffrage (but women still couldn't vote). López reforms represented Liberal modernization agenda, but encountered fierce opposition from Conservatives, Church and landowning class, intensifying political polarization.

events.title: Conservative Return and Rising Tensions
events.description: Conservative candidate Mariano Ospina Pérez elected president, ending 16 years of Liberal rule. However, election results controversial, Liberal split enabled Conservative victory. Political atmosphere increasingly tense, violence between party supporters increased. Conservative government began repressing Liberals, especially in rural areas, foreshadowing imminent 'Violence' period.

events.title: Bogotazo Riots
events.description: Charismatic Liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán assassinated in downtown Bogotá. Gaitán represented populist Liberalism, deeply beloved by working class and peasants, seen as future president. His death triggered 'Bogotazo' riot, Bogotá descended into chaos, mobs burned buildings, looted stores, causing thousands of deaths. Riots spread nationwide. This event marked official beginning of 'La Violencia' period, Colombia descended into decade-long brutal civil war.

events.title: La Violencia
events.description: Colombia descended into devastating political violence, Liberal and Conservative supporters brutally fighting in rural areas. Paramilitary organizations, guerrillas and government forces committed massacres, torture and forced displacement. La Violencia caused approximately 200,000-300,000 deaths, millions displaced. Violence concentrated in coffee-producing regions and Tolima, Cauca Valley, Antioquia provinces. Party extremists demonized opponents, violence became political tool. This period's trauma profoundly affected Colombian society, planting seeds for later armed conflicts.

events.title: Gustavo Rojas Pinilla Coup
events.description: Facing continued violence and political deadlock, Army Commander General Gustavo Rojas Pinilla staged military coup, overthrowing Conservative President Laureano Gómez. Rojas initially welcomed by both parties, hoping he could restore order. Rojas declared amnesty, many guerrillas surrendered. He promoted infrastructure construction including Bogotá international airport and television station. However, Rojas gradually turned dictatorial, repressing dissent, violence didn't end.

events.title: Rojas Fall and National Front Agreement
events.description: Rojas' dictatorial tendencies and economic problems provoked opposition, Liberal and Conservative leaders decided to unite against military rule. Mass protests and military internal opposition forced Rojas to resign and go into exile. In Benidorm, Spain and Sitges, Colombia, party leaders signed 'Frente Nacional' agreement, agreeing to alternately govern for 16 years, equally dividing government positions and congressional seats. This unique political pact aimed to end party violence, restore democracy.

events.title: National Front Begins
events.description: Liberal Alberto Lleras Camargo elected first National Front president. National Front successfully ended large-scale political violence between parties, restored democratic stability. However, two-party monopoly excluded other political forces, limiting genuine competition. Many Violence-era guerrillas felt betrayed, some groups turned to communism, becoming foundation for later armed organizations. National Front brought peace but planted new conflict seeds.

events.title: FARC Founded
events.description: In Marquetalia mountains, communist guerrillas under Pedro Antonio Marín (alias 'Tirofijo' or Manuel Marulanda) resisted government military operation. Subsequently they formed FARC (Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia), claiming to fight for land and social justice for peasants. FARC adopted Mao Zedong and Che Guevara's guerrilla warfare theories, establishing bases in rural areas. FARC became one of Latin America's oldest and most powerful guerrilla organizations, main participant in Colombian armed conflict.

events.title: ELN Founded
events.description: Students and intellectuals inspired by Cuban Revolution established ELN (Ejército de Nacional Liberación) in Santander province. ELN adopted Castro and Che Guevara's revolutionary theories, combining liberation theology. Spanish priest Camilo Torres joined ELN, died in combat 1966, becoming revolutionary martyr and symbol. ELN raised funds through kidnapping, extortion and oil pipeline bombings, mainly active in northeastern mountains.

events.title: M-19 Movement Formed
events.description: In 1970 presidential election, populist movement 'ANAPO' led by former dictator Rojas Pinilla suspected electoral fraud. Dissatisfied radicals formed M-19 guerrilla organization, named after election date. M-19 differed from traditional leftist guerrillas, adopting urban guerrilla tactics, pursuing nationalism and populism rather than Marxism. They conducted high-profile operations attracting media attention, including stealing Bolívar's sword and embassy attacks.

events.title: National Front Ends
events.description: After 16 years, National Front party rotation agreement officially ended. However, Liberal and Conservative parties still dominated political system, continuing to share power and exclude other political forces. National Front brought political stability but also caused political rigidity, elite monopoly and lack of genuine reform. Many social problems like land inequality, poverty and marginalization unresolved, providing soil for continued armed conflict and social discontent.

events.title: Cocaine Empire Rise
events.description: Colombia became world's major cocaine producer and exporter. Medellín and Cali cartels controlled entire industry chain from coca cultivation, processing to smuggling to US and Europe. Pablo Escobar-led Medellín Cartel and Cali Cartel accumulated enormous wealth and power, corrupting government, judiciary and police. Drug trade provided funding for guerrillas and paramilitaries. Cocaine economy profoundly transformed Colombian society, bringing violence, corruption and international pressure, becoming nation's greatest challenge.

events.title: Paramilitary Expansion
events.description: Facing guerrilla threats and government inability to protect property, landowners, ranchers, drug traffickers and military established right-wing paramilitary organizations. These 'Autodefensas' (self-defense forces) under guise of fighting guerrillas, committed massacres, assassinated union leaders, peasant organizers and leftist politicians. Paramilitaries had complex military connections, often receiving tacit approval or support. They controlled land, forcibly displaced peasants, involved in drug trafficking. Paramilitary violence became one of Colombian conflict's most brutal aspects.

events.title: Justice Minister Lara Assassinated
events.description: Justice Minister Rodrigo Lara Bonilla assassinated by Medellín Cartel for actively combating drug cartels. Lara exposed Pablo Escobar's criminal activities and political infiltration, promoted extraditing drug traffickers to US. His killing shocked nation, marking beginning of total war between government and drug traffickers. President Belisario Betancur initiated extradition procedures, traffickers declared 'total war' against state.

events.title: Palace of Justice Siege
events.description: M-19 guerrillas attacked Bogotá Palace of Justice, taking hundreds hostage including Supreme Court justices, demanding government trial. Military stormed building, intense combat and fire killed over 100, including 11 Supreme Court justices. Palace and precious archives destroyed. This tragic event exposed government crisis management failure and military excessive force use. Later investigations revealed forced disappearances and extrajudicial killings, becoming one of Colombia's darkest days.

events.title: Patriotic Union Massacre
events.description: Patriotic Union (Unión Patriótica) was legal party established when FARC participated in peace process, representing leftist participation in democratic politics. However, paramilitaries, drug traffickers and corrupt security forces systematically assassinated Patriotic Union members. From mid-1980s to early 1990s, approximately 3000-5000 Patriotic Union members killed, including two presidential candidates, senators, congressmen and local leaders. This political genocide destroyed left-wing political participation hopes, proving deadly dangers of Colombian democratic space.

events.title: Luis Carlos Galán Assassinated
events.description: Liberal presidential candidate Luis Carlos Galán assassinated at campaign rally by Medellín Cartel. Galán was reformist leader, firmly opposed drug trafficking and corruption, vowing to extradite traffickers. His death was part of traffickers' 'terrorism' offensive against state. Galán's killing shocked nation, deepening political crisis. Succeeding President César Gaviria intensified anti-trafficking efforts, but drug violence continued escalating.

events.title: Drug Terrorism Peak
events.description: Medellín Cartel launched terror offensive against government, judiciary and public, opposing extradition. They bombed Avianca flight (killing 107), bombed DAS (security agency) headquarters, bombed shopping centers and banks, kidnapped politicians, journalists and celebrity family members. Bogotá and Medellín gripped by fear. Government offered 'surrender for reduced sentences' policy, promising not to extradite self-surrendering traffickers. This period called 'drug war,' causing thousands of deaths, severely damaging state institutions and public confidence.

events.title: Seventh Ballot Movement
events.description: Young students launched 'Séptima Papeleta' movement, demanding constituent assembly to reform outdated 1886 constitution. Movement gained widespread support, Supreme Court ruled voting legal. In 1990, Colombians voted in favor of constituent assembly. 70 delegates (including former M-19 guerrillas, indigenous people and different political factions) drafted new constitution. This was rare success of civil society pushing political reform, reflecting dissatisfaction with existing system and desire for change.

events.title: New Constitution Promulgated
events.description: Colombia promulgated new constitution, replacing 105-year-old 1886 constitution. New constitution was one of Latin America's most progressive, guaranteeing broad human rights, establishing Constitutional Court, strengthening judicial independence, recognizing indigenous and Afro-Colombian rights, protecting environment, establishing tutela (people's action) mechanism to protect fundamental rights. Constitution prohibited extraditing nationals. Though constitution brought many progressive reforms, in reality of continued violence and conflict, many provisions difficult to implement.

events.title: Pablo Escobar Surrenders
events.description: Facing pressure from government, rival Cali Cartel and 'Los Pepes' (anti-Escobar alliance of paramilitaries, police and traffickers), Pablo Escobar surrendered to government. In exchange, government promised no extradition, allowing Escobar to serve sentence in self-built 'La Catedral' prison. Cathedral actually luxury estate, Escobar continued running criminal empire. When government attempted transferring him to real prison, Escobar escaped, continuing as fugitive.

events.title: Death of Pablo Escobar
events.description: After 16-month manhunt, Colombian National Police Search Bloc shot dead Pablo Escobar in Medellín residential house. Escobar's death marked Medellín Cartel's end, but didn't end Colombian drug trade. Cali Cartel took over market, later Norte del Valle Cartel and Mexican cartels became major players. Escobar left complex legacy: to some brutal criminal, to others (especially Medellín slum residents) philanthropist and Robin Hood-like figure.

events.title: Cali Cartel Collapse
events.description: With US support, Colombian government arrested Cali Cartel main leaders including Rodríguez Orejuela brothers. Cali Cartel controlled about 80% of global cocaine trade, but was more low-profile than Medellín Cartel, emphasizing bribery over violence. However, discovery of Cali Cartel funding President Ernesto Samper's campaign scandal ('Proceso 8000') severely damaged government credibility. After Cali Cartel collapse, drug trade fragmented into smaller 'boutique' cartels and paramilitary organizations.

events.title: FARC Military Expansion
events.description: Leveraging drug money and government weakness, FARC conducted largest military expansion, growing from about 5000 to nearly 20,000 fighters. FARC shifted from small-scale guerrilla warfare to large-scale operations, attacking military bases, controlling vast territories (especially southern jungles and rural areas), kidnapping politicians, military and civilians for ransom. FARC achieved major military victories at Mitú, Barrancabermeja and other regions, defeating government forces. This was FARC's power peak, seemed state might collapse or be forced to negotiate major concessions.

events.title: Peace Process and Demilitarized Zone
events.description: President Andrés Pastrana negotiated peace with FARC, establishing 42,000 square kilometer demilitarized zone (Zona de Despeje) as negotiation site, effectively FARC-controlled state within state. However, FARC used demilitarized zone to regroup militarily, kidnap hostages and cultivate coca. Negotiations stalled, FARC kidnapped senators and continued attacks. In 2002, Pastrana declared negotiation failure, military reentered demilitarized zone. Peace process failure deepened public skepticism about negotiations, paving way for hardliner rise.

events.title: AUC Founded
events.description: Regional paramilitary organizations unified under Carlos Castaño's leadership as AUC (Autodefensas Unidas de Colombia), becoming national right-wing paramilitary alliance. AUC claimed to protect civilians from guerrilla threats, but committed large-scale massacres, forced displacement and drug trafficking. AUC had secret military cooperation, funded by landowners and businessmen. AUC became one of conflict's most brutal actors, especially targeting civilian communities suspected of guerrilla support.

events.title: Álvaro Uribe Elected
events.description: Álvaro Uribe Vélez elected president with hardline security policy, promising 'Democratic Security' strategy, militarily defeating guerrillas to restore state authority. Uribe's father killed by FARC, he enjoyed middle-class and elite support, tired of endless violence and kidnappings. Uribe represented break with past negotiation policies, arguing only overwhelming military force could achieve peace. He became Colombia's most influential and controversial 21st century leader.

events.title: Plan Colombia and Military Buildup
events.description: With US 'Plan Colombia' support, Colombian military underwent massive modernization and expansion. US provided billions in military aid, training, equipment and intelligence support, nominally fighting drugs but actually also combating guerrillas. Military numbers doubled, purchased helicopters and advanced weapons, improved intelligence capabilities. Uribe increased defense spending, established 'peasant soldier' networks and mobile brigades. Military buildup changed battlefield power balance, FARC shifted from offensive to defensive.

events.title: AUC Demobilization Process
events.description: Uribe government negotiated AUC demobilization, promising lenient 'Justice and Peace Law.' About 31,000 paramilitary fighters nominally demobilized. However, process highly controversial: short sentences (5-8 years), insufficient truth revelation, limited reparations, many commanders extradited to US for drug charges rather than facing war crimes in Colombia. Many demobilized paramilitaries reorganized as 'criminal organizations' (BACRIM), continuing drug trafficking and violence. Demobilization didn't truly end paramilitary phenomenon.

events.title: Parapolitics Scandal
events.description: 'Parapolítica' scandal exposed evidence of dozens of congressmen, governors and politicians colluding with AUC. Supreme Court investigations showed many Uribe allies had paramilitary connections, signing secret agreements for electoral support and funding. Over 60 congressmen investigated or convicted. Scandal exposed Colombian political corruption depth and paramilitary state institution infiltration extent, severely damaging Uribe government credibility, but Uribe himself maintained high approval ratings.

events.title: Ecuador Border Raid
events.description: Colombian military crossed into Ecuador, bombing FARC camp, killing second-in-command leader Raúl Reyes. Operation obtained valuable intelligence from Reyes' computers, but unauthorized cross-border operation triggered diplomatic crisis. Ecuador President Rafael Correa and Venezuela's Hugo Chávez condemned 'aggression,' both countries briefly broke diplomatic relations with Colombia. Incident highlighted Colombian conflict's regional impact and tensions with neighbors.

events.title: FARC Major Setbacks
events.description: FARC suffered series of devastating blows. Besides Reyes killed, founder and supreme commander Manuel Marulanda ('Tirofijo') died from heart attack, having led FARC in jungles for over 40 years. In July, military conducted 'Operation Jaque,' disguised as humanitarian organization, rescuing 15 hostages without firing shot, including former presidential candidate Íngrid Betancourt and three US contractors. These events marked FARC's decline from peak, military and political prestige severely damaged.

events.title: Juan Manuel Santos Elected
events.description: Juan Manuel Santos, Uribe's former defense minister, elected president, promising to continue Uribe's security policies. However, Santos quickly showed different direction, hinting willingness to negotiate with FARC. Santos believed military pressure had weakened FARC to point where peace negotiable. This shift surprised many Uribe supporters, Uribe himself later became fierce critic of Santos' peace process.

events.title: FARC Top Leader Alfonso Cano Killed
events.description: Military killed FARC supreme leader Alfonso Cano (real name Guillermo León Sáenz) in Cauca province mountains. Cano was FARC's first non-peasant origin leader, intellectual and ideologue. His death was another major blow to FARC, leadership transferred to more pragmatic Rodrigo Londoño (alias 'Timochenko'). New leadership more willing to consider peace negotiations, paving way for 2012 talks opening.

events.title: Peace Negotiations with FARC Begin
events.description: Santos government began formal peace negotiations with FARC in Havana, Cuba (later partly in Oslo, Norway). Talks secretly prepared for months, guaranteed by Cuba and Norway, Venezuela and Chile as observers. Negotiation agenda included six points: rural land reform, political participation, ending conflict, drug problem, victim rights and implementation mechanisms. Unlike past, no ceasefire or demilitarized zone, negotiations conducted while conflict continued, showing both sides' pragmatic attitude and determination to reach agreement.

events.title: Santos Reelection and Peace Mandate
events.description: Presidential election became referendum on peace process. Santos faced former ally Uribe-backed hardliner candidate Óscar Iván Zuluaga. Election intense, first round Zuluaga led, but Santos narrowly won second round. Victory viewed as voters' narrow support for peace negotiations, but also showed nation severely divided on peace issue. Santos after reelection accelerated negotiation process, determined to reach agreement.

events.title: Final Peace Agreement with FARC
events.description: After nearly four years of negotiations, government and FARC reached final peace agreement in Havana, ending over 52-year armed conflict. Agreement included FARC disarmament, transformation into legal political party, rural reform, truth and justice transitional mechanisms, victim reparations and social reintegration programs. In September, Santos and FARC leader Timochenko held historic signing ceremony in Cartagena. Agreement hailed as milestone in Latin American peace processes, but faced fierce domestic opposition.

events.title: Peace Agreement Referendum Fails
events.description: In binding referendum, Colombian voters rejected peace agreement by narrow margin 50.2% to 49.8%, shocking world. Opposition led by former President Uribe criticized agreement too lenient on FARC, sentences too light, allowing guerrillas into politics without prison. Turnout only 37%, Caribbean coast conflict-affected regions supported peace, but inland cities (like Bogotá, Medellín) opposed dominated. Referendum result was blow to Santos, but he vowed to save peace process.

events.title: Revised Agreement and Congressional Approval
events.description: After referendum failure, government and FARC renegotiated, incorporating some opposition concerns, revised agreement strengthened crime punishment and limited political participation. Unable to hold another referendum, Santos submitted revised agreement to Congress for approval, Congress passed with overwhelming majority. Approval process sparked constitutional controversy (bypassing direct democracy), but Santos insisted must advance peace. In December, revised agreement officially signed in Bogotá, FARC began disarmament process.

events.title: Santos Wins Nobel Peace Prize
events.description: Nobel Committee awarded Juan Manuel Santos Nobel Peace Prize, recognizing his 'resolute efforts to end Colombia's more than 50-year civil war.' Despite referendum failure, committee praised Santos' persistence in peace process, believing he made decisive contribution to peace. Prize elevated Santos' international reputation, but domestic reaction polarized: supporters celebrated, opponents (especially Uribe supporters) criticized, believing FARC should be punished not negotiated with.

events.title: FARC Disarmament
events.description: FARC fighters surrendered weapons in 26 concentration zones nationwide under UN supervision. About 7000 guerrillas participated in disarmament and demobilization process, UN collected weapons and melted them into peace monuments. FARC officially dissolved as guerrilla organization, transforming into legal political party 'Fuerza Alternativa Revolucionaria del Común' (keeping FARC acronym). This was turning point in Colombian history, ending one of Western Hemisphere's longest guerrilla wars.

events.title: Iván Duque Elected
events.description: Right-wing candidate Iván Duque elected president with Uribe support, defeating leftist former Bogotá mayor Gustavo Petro. Duque criticized peace agreement, promising to modify or abolish parts, especially transitional justice mechanisms. His victory reflected many Colombians' dissatisfaction with peace agreement and continued skepticism of left. However, Duque faced international pressure and constitutional obligations to implement peace agreement, though he delayed and weakened many provisions.

events.title: FARC Dissidents Rearm
events.description: Some former FARC commanders announced rearming, rejecting peace agreement, accusing government of not fulfilling promises, former fighters assassinated, rural reform unimplemented. Former FARC negotiator Iván Márquez and Jesús Santrich led 'Segunda Marquetalia' organization. Though dissident numbers limited (hundreds to thousand), rearming was blow to peace process, showing implementation challenges. Most former FARC members remained committed to peace, but many assassinated or living in poverty and marginalization.

events.title: National Strike and Social Unrest
events.description: Colombia erupted in massive national strike and protests against Duque government's economic policies, labor reforms, pension cuts, social leader assassinations and poor peace agreement implementation. Protests lasted weeks, attracting students, unions, indigenous people and masses. Government repression caused deaths and injuries, intensifying tensions. Protests reflected Colombia's deep social discontent: inequality, poverty, unemployment, corruption and elite disconnection from people. Duque's approval ratings plummeted, social polarization deepened.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Impact
events.description: COVID-19 pandemic severely hit Colombia, causing tens of thousands of deaths, severe economic recession, soaring unemployment, increased poverty. Duque government implemented strict lockdowns, but limited economic relief, millions fell into poverty. Pandemic exposed healthcare system weaknesses and social inequality. Informal economy workers severely affected. Pandemic also disrupted peace agreement implementation, rural violence continued, illegal armed groups (including ELN, FARC dissidents and criminal organizations) filled power vacuum.

events.title: National Strike and Violent Repression
events.description: Protests against Duque government tax reform evolved into months-long national uprising, becoming Colombia's largest social unrest in decades. Protesters demanded tax justice, healthcare reform, education investment and end to violence. Police and military violently repressed, causing at least 80 deaths, thousands injured and arrested, numerous sexual violence and torture reports. Cali and other cities became resistance centers, youth blocked roads, established 'resistance points.' International community condemned violence. Strike eventually subsided, but showed Colombian social crisis and institutional legitimacy crisis.

events.title: Gustavo Petro Historic Victory
events.description: Leftist former guerrilla, former Bogotá mayor Gustavo Petro elected Colombian president, first leftist president in nation's history. Petro was M-19 guerrilla member, later turned to democratic politics. His running mate Francia Márquez became first Afro-Colombian female vice president. Petro promised 'change,' promoting social justice, environmental protection, full peace agreement implementation, ELN negotiations and combating inequality. Victory reflected voters' rejection of traditional elites and desire for change, marking historic Colombian political transformation.

events.title: Petro's Total Peace Policy
events.description: Petro government launched 'Paz Total' (Total Peace) strategy, simultaneously negotiating with all illegal armed groups: ELN guerrillas, FARC dissidents, 'Clan del Golfo' and other criminal organizations. Government resumed formal negotiations with ELN (in Venezuela, Cuba and Mexico), reaching temporary ceasefire. Petro sought to address violence roots rather than pure military confrontation, emphasizing social investment and rural development. However, policy faced challenges: armed group fragmentation, ceasefire violations, and right-wing opposition accusing Petro of surrendering to criminals.

events.title: Social Reforms and Political Resistance
events.description: Petro promoted ambitious reform agenda: healthcare system reform, pension reform, labor reform, land reform and energy transition (from fossil fuels to renewables). However, reforms faced fierce resistance in Congress, even though Petro coalition controlled majority. Reforms criticized as too radical or poorly implemented. Petro had tense relations with judiciary, media and opposition, accused of authoritarian tendencies. Approval ratings fluctuated, economic challenges and inflation persisted.

events.title: Contemporary Colombia: Challenges and Transformation
events.description: In 2024, Colombia at crucial transformation moment. Petro government strives to achieve 'historic change' but faces enormous challenges. Peace process incomplete: FARC agreement implementation slow, over 350 former fighters assassinated, rural reform lagging. ELN negotiations fluctuating, rural violence continues, illegal armed groups fighting for territory and drug routes. Coca cultivation and cocaine production at historic highs. Economic difficulties: inflation, unemployment, inequality remain severe. About 40% of population living in poverty. Venezuelan refugee crisis (about 2.5 million refugees) pressuring Colombia. However, hopeful signs: first leftist government governing peacefully, democratic resilience, youth and women activism, cultural flourishing (Colombia is Latin music powerhouse, Bogotá and Medellín becoming innovation and entrepreneurship hubs). Colombia stands at crossroads: can it achieve true peace and social justice, or continue cycle of violence and inequality? This is decisive decade.
